title: Tales of genetics: Powerlifting Genius
summary: First of his 'tales' about exceptional people from his years in commercial gyms: a natural beginner of average build who, with a minimalist linear progression and no real program, reached near-450 squat within about six months and later a 365 bench and 500 squat in about 1-1.5 years. He uses it to argue that elite strength is mostly genetic, while urging viewers not to quit.

claims.claim: At his strongest, when focused on powerlifting and heaviest, he weighed 225 lbs with a 335 bench, 500 deadlift and a 400-something squat.
The 'genius' was a former athlete new to lifting, around 190-200 lbs and about 5'8", with average limb lengths and no obvious powerlifting leverages.
He reached a 275 bench single and was nearing a four-plate squat very quickly after starting, far faster than NH, who took much longer to bench 275.
He trained minimally: one compound, a few back-off sets, sometimes leaving within an hour; no program, no special nutrition, pure linear progression, no accessories or variations, no sleeves.
Within about six months of picking up a barbell he got close to a 450 squat.
His definition of strength giftedness: making constant progress on a very simplistic program with no plateaus, while most people plateau around 200 lbs or approaching three plates on the squat.

The guy, known to be natural, later had a 365 bench and 500 squat, roughly 2x bodyweight bench and nearly 3x bodyweight squat, in about a year to a year and a half without any program, in his early 20s.
The first time he deadlifted he did 315 for 8 easily; NH believes he could pull 600 within two years.
People who break world records and win in powerlifting are genetic outliers like this; if you struggled to deadlift four plates or bench 225, elite strength is not for you, and NH includes himself.
Some people use PEDs for 20 years at 200+ lbs bodyweight and still can't bench 365.
Genetic freaks get bigger and stronger faster with less effort, rarely get injured and care less about form, and there is nothing you can do about it.
Don't use genetic outliers as an excuse to quit: if you love powerlifting keep chasing it, since someone better will always exist; work hard and grind for yourself.
He admits he once felt it was unfair that someone could walk in and get numbers he had worked so long for, but accepts that's life.
He describes himself as standoffish at the gym and rarely talking to people.
